skyline.text: Why Amit Varma says inflation hurts the poor the most
How rising prices eat away at deals written in rupees
A finance minister defers to his rivals’ finest minds

footnote.text: We’re not getting any money for this. It’s a labour of love.

brief.head: Nothing wholesale
brief.text: The Wholesale Price Index is not wholesale and reflects nobody’s basket, Ajay Shah said, hence the nickel in it. Use the CPI, and the WPI’s prices as a database. {068-C04}

brief.head: Checking the CPI
brief.text: Ajay Shah distrusts government data by default. But when he and Ila Patnaik checked the CPI’s weights and prices against independent data, both broadly matched. {068-S02}

brief.head: Polls and low rates
brief.text: In advanced economies’ data, Ajay Shah said, government-controlled central banks keep rates low before elections to create a feel-good mood. The inflation comes later. {#election}

brief.head: A car that turns late
brief.text: A rate change works with a long lag, Ajay Shah said, like a car that turns long after you move the wheel. So central banks must forecast. {068-C12}

brief.text: A 2 per cent target leaves little room to cut rates, Ajay Shah said, and India’s financial system is weak. Hence 4 per cent, plus or minus 2. {068-C13}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on taming rising prices
lead.head: How India learnt to love a target
body: Amit Varma started with apples. If maggots ruin the orchard that feeds a town, he said, apples get dearer. That is supply and demand, not inflation, which is when nearly everything goes up at once.

It happens, he said, when the quantity of money changes and the goods and services stay the same. “Milton Friedman once famously said inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon,” Varma said. {068-C01}
Because the new money is not shared out in proportion to what people already have, the poor suffer most. “Inflation is a tax on the poor,” Varma said. {068-C02}

From there Ajay Shah, who was part of the policy community that made inflation targeting happen in India, took over. His case was that low and stable inflation matters far more than it seems, and that India finally got the machinery for it right.
## The hidden costs
Inflation is not the price of growth, Shah argued. It gets in the way of growth, in three ways.

First, it scrambles signals. Firms read a changing world through prices. When apples get dearer, a firm cannot tell whether they are scarce, wanted more, or simply caught up in inflation. “The deep insight is that high inflation messes with the information processing problem of firms,” he said. {068-C05}

Second, it eats contracts. Firms bind themselves to one another through deals written in rupees, and inflation forces them to renegotiate though nothing real has changed. That burns the effort they need for real change. {068-C06}

Third, it shortens sight. “In an environment with high and variable inflation, the future gets reduced into the present,” Shah said. {068-C07} People stop planning beyond a couple of years, and the long projects that bring growth suffer.
Growth, Varma added, is “the greatest god”, because only growth gets a nation out of poverty. {068-C08}
## A target with teeth
Chasing anything else, Shah said, always comes at the cost of one task. “The core dharma of a central bank is to deliver low and stable inflation.” {068-C09}

The way to hold it to that job came from New Zealand in 1987: an inflation target written into law by parliament, which grants the central bank its power over money. New Zealand even paid senior central bank staff a bonus for hitting it. {#nz1987}
Today, Shah said, all the advanced economies target inflation, though “some of them are too polite or too cheap to offer a bonus”.
## India’s way
In India, Shah was discussing inflation targeting with Yashwant Sinha as early as 2002. {068-S04}
The 2007 boom, when the RBI bought dollars to hold down the rupee and flooded the economy with money, ended in an inflation crisis that won the argument among economists. {068-S05}
When the draft law stalled, Shah and KP Krishnan borrowed a 1990s trick: a signed agreement between the finance ministry and the RBI. {068-S07}
P. Chidambaram left the decision to his successor; Arun Jaitley said yes overnight. The agreement was signed on 20 February 2015, and in 2016 the RBI Act was amended to make inflation targeting law.
The amendment struck out the words that had described the RBI since 1934: “as a temporary measure”. {068-S10}
Varma’s parting advice was never to normalise anything or take the world for granted. “We’ve got to preserve the little good that we have done in the world,” he said. {068-R01}

second.label: The RBI Act
second.head: The stopgap that grew up
second.deck: In 2016, the RBI Act finally said what the central bank is for
body: When the British created the Reserve Bank of India in 1934, Ajay Shah said, “they correctly understood that they don’t understand”. {#rbi1934} The preamble said the international monetary system was too disorganised to settle India’s monetary arrangements.

So the bank was created “as a temporary measure”. The words survived until 2016, when the amendment that wrote inflation targeting into the RBI Act replaced them with “in order to deliver price stability”. {068-S10}
Shah relished the change. His one regret was that the agreement behind it, signed on 20 February 2015 by Rajiv Mehrishi and Raghuram Rajan, was not done as a public show. {#feb2015}

quote.text: on his forehead was the word, you’re a temporary measure, because we haven’t yet figured out what to do.

second.caption: the RBI’s temporary preamble

third.head: A house for a loaf
body: Germany after the First World War, Amit Varma said, is a great example of hyperinflation. The winning nations demanded reparations so high that Germany had no option but to print tons of money.
Prices went completely out of whack: what could buy a house one week, Varma said, bought a loaf of bread the next. The chaos fed the right-wing extremism that produced Adolf Hitler.

John Maynard Keynes wrote about it at the time in *The Economic Consequences of the Peace*. {068-R03} One reason for such crazy demands, Keynes pointed out, was that nobody knew national wealth. {068-S01}
That gap, Varma said, created the demand for something like GDP, which did not then exist. “That’s a whole different story,” he added, pointing listeners to his own episode on GDP.

sections.label: The basics
sections.head: Too much money, too few goods
sections.caption: inflation as a tax on the poor
body: Amit Varma set out to explain inflation in the simplest terms, a “really dumbed down, simplistic version”, for anyone who had never thought about it before.

Prices are set by supply and demand. If maggots ruin the orchard that grows a town’s apples, apples get dearer. That is not inflation. Inflation is when tomatoes, onions and mobile phones all go up together.

Picture money on one side and goods and services on the other, he said, held in balance by prices. If the government prints twenty per cent more money and the goods stay the same, everything costs more. {#twenty}
## Who pays the bill

The state has a monopoly on money. A government can print it to fund popular schemes, and everyone says the government is doing so much: it works politically. But prices rise for everyone, and the new money is not shared in proportion to what people already have. {068-C02}
So the poor suffer most, Varma said. “If there is rampant inflation, you have to hold your government accountable.”
Varma leaned on Milton Friedman’s famous line that inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon. {068-C01}
~ Governments no longer literally print money, he noted. The central bank, which holds the monopoly, can steer the money supply through interest rates, so inflation is directly in its control.

quote.text: inevitably the poor are the greatest sufferers, which is why I keep reminding people, inflation is a tax on the poor.

sections.label: The measure
sections.head: Bacon, bread and the basket
sections.caption: how inflation is measured
body: Start with your own shopping, Ajay Shah said. Multiply the quantity of each thing you buy by its price, add it all up, and do it again next month with new prices.
For Amit Varma, a “good devout non vegetarian”, that means vast amounts of bacon and tiny amounts of bread. {#bacon}
Some prices rise and some fall, and on average that noise cancels out. “The average overall systematic increase in the cost of your basket is your inflation,” Shah said. {068-C03}
## The national basket

Statisticians do the same for the whole country. Vast household surveys supply the weights: the CMIE survey covers about 190,000 households three times a year, asking about some 90 items. {068-R11} The weights stay fixed for a couple of years, and each month’s prices are plugged in.
The result, the consumer price index, matches nobody’s life exactly, but it reflects the average household.
Shah is sceptical of government data by default. But when he and Ila Patnaik cross-checked the CPI’s weights and prices against independent sources, both broadly held up. {068-S02}
~ The Wholesale Price Index is another matter, he warned. It has nothing wholesale about it and reflects nobody’s basket. “What human being eats nickel?” {068-J03}

quote.text: Use the CPI. CPI is a decent good index and it is meaningful.

sections.label: The costs
sections.head: Static on the dashboard
sections.caption: why inflation matters
body: Is a point or two of inflation really a problem? Ajay Shah began with the price system, and a world that, as in “either Hindu or Buddhist philosophy”, is ever changing. {068-J07}

Tastes and technology shift, and firms read those shifts through prices and adapt. “In the use of knowledge in society, the heavy lifting is being done by prices,” Shah said, echoing Friedrich Hayek’s essay. “Now don’t put noise into prices.” {068-R06}

Inflation does exactly that. A firm seeing dearer apples cannot tell if apples are scarce or prices are simply rising, and high inflation is also variable inflation. Firms are misled into wrong adjustments. {068-C05}
## Muscle and acid
Adjusting is exhausting, and every firm has a finite budget of what Shah called adjustment muscle. Inflation forces firms to renegotiate contracts written in rupees, though nothing real has changed.

Shah’s example was a contract paying Amit Varma ten lakh rupees an episode “to the great podcaster”. Varma assured listeners that the hosts are paid nothing: “It’s a labour of love.” {068-J04} After nine per cent inflation, Shah imagined Varma grumbling that “Mr BeerBiceps” is paid much better.
~ The third cost falls on the future. With high and variable inflation, Shah said, “your planning horizon shrinks”, and the long, complex projects that bring growth go unbuilt. {068-C07}

quote.text: high and variable inflation is the acid that drips on these contracts and destroys their meaning.

sections.label: The target
sections.head: Power, meet accountability
sections.caption: making central banks accountable
body: Parliament gives the central bank the power to create fiat money, Ajay Shah said, and a basic rule of public administration is that every grant of power comes with checks. {068-C10}
Being appointed to run a central bank does not make anyone a good guy. That, he said, is simple public choice theory.

Central banks have a long history of failure. The fix came from New Zealand in 1987: an inflation target written into law, with a bonus for senior staff who hit it. {#nz1987} Parliament is the principal; the central bank is its agent.

Shah recalled Keynes wishing that economists would be humble like dentists, a line that, he said, always gets applied to central bankers. {068-J08} Treat the central bank like a dentist, he said: do the root canal well, and you get a bonus.
## Between two extremes
Amit Varma called the target elegant. A central bank run by the government would do populist things; one left to do whatever it wants could be captured by special interests.
Shah spelt out both dangers. Government control brings an election business cycle. At the other extreme are economists who think public choice theory applies to everyone but themselves. {068-C11}
~ The target sits between the two, Varma said: define one job, stay out of the way, and hold the bank to account if it misses.

quote.text: But for us, we’re good guys and we should be given a free hand and we should do whatever we want.

sections.label: The boiler room
sections.head: One lever, slow steering
sections.caption: the central bank’s single lever
body: Good central banks, Ajay Shah said, tinker with only one price: the short-term interest rate. Long-term rates, the exchange rate and equity prices are left to the market. “In all modern central banks, we are all Wicksellian now.” {068-J10}
The difficulty is the lag. A rate change works on inflation slowly, like a car that responds long after you turn the wheel, so a central bank has to forecast rather than react. {068-C12}
In India, Shah admitted, the models are abysmal, so the central bank may have little choice but to respond to the present.
## Brakes and accelerator
In a boom, inflation tends to rise and the central bank raises rates. Home loans, car loans and corporate debt get dearer, and the economy cools. It is meant to watch inflation, not the boom.
In a crisis it cuts. The day India announced the world’s most extensive COVID lockdown, Shah said, nobody needed a model to see trouble ahead, and the RBI rightly brought rates down fast. {#covid}
~ The booms Shah had in mind were 1997 and 2007. Young listeners who missed them, he lamented, “have no idea what economic success looks like”. {068-J13}

quote.text: In the engine room, there’s only one joystick where you’re controlling the short term rate. It’s one scalar, so not even a joystick.

sections.label: The India story
sections.head: A band, not a bullseye
sections.caption: India’s target and the old RBI
body: Why 4 per cent, when advanced economies aim for 2? Zero is out, Amit Varma noted, for fear of deflation. But 2, Ajay Shah said, is perilously close to zero, and a central bank cannot usefully cut rates below it.
India also has a deeply broken financial system that muffles rate changes. Where a sophisticated system needs a 25 or 50 basis point move, India needs bigger ones, and so more headroom. {#basis}
Weak transmission rules out precision too. “It is an unreasonable task to ask the central bank that get me precisely 4.00,” Shah said. Hence a band of 2 to 6 per cent. {068-C13}
Two quarters outside the band oblige the RBI to explain in public what went wrong. Varma relished hearing “central banker” and “penitent” in the same sentence. {068-J12}
## The old RBI
Getting there took years. In the bad old days, Shah said, the RBI was not a real central bank but a central planning agency, a handmaiden of the government. {068-S03}
C. Rangarajan and deputy governor Tarapore rethought it in the 1990s. Then the RBI slid into a long socialist period, and the thinking moved to academia and the Ministry of Finance.
~ Shah summed up that period’s attitude with Montagu Norman, the former Bank of England governor: “I don’t have reasons, I have my instincts.” {068-J09}

quote.text: Like really, when you look at it, it was just an awful central planning organization with little by way of redeeming features.

side.boxText: Amit Varma opened with Milton Friedman’s famous line that inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon. Ajay Shah traced the deeper insight, that inflation scrambles the price signals firms rely on, to Friedman’s 1968 paper, *The Role of Monetary Policy*. {#friedman1968}

contQuote.text: We achieved something beautiful called inflation targeting. It took a while, we got there. It is one rare, elegant piece of great legislation, but these things are always under threat.

p3.title: Inside the reform
p3.deck: Four tales of how inflation targeting won its long argument in India

stories.start: to tell that story again because it's such a beautiful story
stories.end: And for me, this is actually the end, because this never happens again
stories.caption: Arun Jaitley’s overnight yes
stories.kicker: Amit Varma retells a story from his KP Krishnan episode
stories.head: Who am I to argue?
body: By the end of 2013 or early 2014, as Ajay Shah remembered it, a draft Monetary Policy Framework Agreement sat with the finance minister, P. Chidambaram. It had been worked over by KP Krishnan and Chidambaram, and discussed with Montek Ahluwalia and Manmohan Singh.

Chidambaram wrote on the file that it was one of the most important milestones in the history of India. But it should not be the work of a lame-duck government, he wrote, and he left it to his successor, correctly predicting that it would not be him. {068-S08}
The successor was Arun Jaitley. Amit Varma retold what happened next as Krishnan had told it to him, in an episode Varma called an “eight hour masterpiece”. {#eighthour}
Krishnan handed the new minister the file, perhaps on the evening of the same day, and told him it was really big. The next morning Jaitley called: yes, let’s do it.
Krishnan was alarmed. He wanted it done, but this was far-reaching. It changed everything. Had the minister actually read it?

Jaitley, a little irritated, said he had gone through it. Then he made his point: “If this country’s finest economic mind and finest legal mind have said that this must be done, then who am I to argue?” He meant Manmohan Singh and P. Chidambaram. {068-S09}

~ For Varma this was grace across party lines, and it was also an ending. “This never happens again,” he said. Politics, in his telling, changed forever, and today on every side of the aisle there is “just a different class of people”.
stories.why: Years of reform work cleared their last hurdle because one politician deferred to his opponents’ expertise. Trust across party lines, the story suggests, is a kind of institutional capital, and it can disappear quietly.
stories.postscript: In 2016 the RBI Act was amended to build in inflation targeting and a monetary policy committee.

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a reform that had to wait its turn
stories.head: Too early, said the minister
body: In 2002, years before the idea became law, Ajay Shah was already talking to Yashwant Sinha about inflation targeting. {068-S04}

These ideas, Sinha said, were way ahead of anything India’s intelligentsia was discussing. They would need to become much more normal in Indian intellectual debate before some future finance minister could act on them.
Shah accepted the point. “Point well taken,” he said, looking back. “This is the way it should be done.”

~ The RBI of the day, Shah said, wanted detailed control of the financial system and the exchange rate, and no accountability for inflation. Until the argument was won, the thinking lived in academia and the Ministry of Finance.
stories.why: A reform must win the argument in public debate long before it can win in government. That journey through the pipeline, Amit Varma said, is the subject of the hosts’ episode *The Long Road to Change*. {068-R09}

stories.start: And then in the uh mid-2000s, in the 2007 boom, uh the working
stories.end: cannot just be accepted in the modern world. You now need to do better
stories.caption: the 2007 boom
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the boom that discredited the old RBI
stories.head: Buying dollars, printing trouble
body: In the go-go years of the mid-2000s, the economy was booming and foreign capital poured into India, as it does when times are good. The rupee ought to have risen.
Instead, Ajay Shah said, the RBI tried to fix the exchange rate by buying up the dollars, and it paid for them in rupees. {068-S05}
“And so the local economy got flooded with rupees,” Shah said. “And so it was expansionary monetary policy at the worst possible time. And that generated a nice big inflation crisis.”
~ By and large, he said, that won the case among economists. The old RBI could not just be accepted in the modern world; India needed to do better.
stories.why: A central bank that tries to steer the exchange rate gives up control of inflation. Pursue any other objective, Shah argued earlier in the episode, and you will always end up sacrificing the core one: low and stable inflation. {068-C09}

stories.start: KP Krishna and I were talking, we were kicking ideas around
stories.end: So that's how the monetary policy framework agreement was drafted
stories.caption: the Ways and Means trick
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on borrowing a trick from the 1990s
stories.head: Four emails an hour
body: In 2013 the draft Indian Financial Code was stuck: P. Chidambaram said it was too big to pass so late in his government’s term. Ajay Shah, travelling abroad, and KP Krishnan traded “four emails per hour” on what to do. {#emails}

They remembered the 1990s, when Parliament could not pass a law to stop the RBI printing money for deficits. Instead the finance ministry and the RBI signed the Ways and Means Agreement, with Montek Ahluwalia and C. Rangarajan at a public ceremony. {068-S07}
Shah and Krishnan proposed the same for inflation: a Monetary Policy Framework Agreement, in which the RBI would commit to a target and the government would not push it in other directions.
~ Amit Varma suggested the first deal benefited from those two particular people being in office. A less enlightened RBI governor, he said, might have pushed back.
stories.why: When the legislative route is blocked, a public, signed commitment between the two parties can deliver the reform first. The law, Shah noted, followed later, when the right time came.

quiz.q: Why, according to Amit Varma, does inflation hit the poor hardest?
quiz.a: New money isn’t shared out in proportion to what people already have.

quiz.q: What three things did Ajay Shah say every reader must know about the Wholesale Price Index?
quiz.a: Nothing wholesale about it, meaningless as an index, but a useful price database.

quiz.q: Which country invented inflation targeting in 1987, and how did it reward central bankers?
quiz.a: New Zealand, which paid senior central bank staff a bonus for hitting it.

quiz.q: Why did India choose a 4 per cent target instead of the 2 per cent common elsewhere?
quiz.a: More room to cut rates in a slump, with a weak financial system.

quiz.q: What did the RBI do during the 2007 boom that set off an inflation crisis?
quiz.a: It bought dollars to stop the rupee rising, flooding the economy with rupees.

quiz.q: Which words did the 2016 amendment remove from the 1934 RBI Act’s preamble?
quiz.a: “As a temporary measure”, replaced with “in order to deliver price stability”.
